results.caption:
Running in extreme heat has some benefits. ☀️ 🔥 

At least that’s what I kept telling myself while questioning every decision that led me to this moment.

But there actually is science behind heat training.

Repeated, controlled exercise in the heat can lead to heat acclimation, including:

🔥 Increased plasma volume:
helping support stroke volume and cardiovascular stability.

🔥 Improved cooling:
your body adapts with improved sweating and skin blood-flow responses.

🔥 Reduced cardiovascular strain:
once acclimated, heart rate and core temperature can be lower at the same workload in the heat.

🔥 Better heat tolerance & performance:
systematic reviews show heat acclimation can improve exercise capacity and performance in hot environments.

But here’s the important part:

One miserable (but magical) run in the heat doesn’t magically make you better.

These adaptations develop through repeated, progressive heat exposure, commonly over roughly 1–2 weeks. And deliberately dehydrating yourself isn’t the goal. Dehydration increases physiological strain and can hurt performance.

And what about calories?

Running in the heat can increase physiological stress at a given workload, but there isn’t good reason to treat extreme heat as some kind of calorie-burning or fat-loss hack. If the heat forces you to slow down, any difference in total energy expenditure is, at most, negligible.

So, that 4 lbs you “lost” after your hot run?

Congratulations. You just sweat your ass off. 😂

Heat training can be a useful tool. But heat exhaustion is not a training adaptation.

And nothing completes the experience quite like finishing a brutally hot run with a lukewarm electrolyte drink. 🤌 Thanks @drinkhoist 

Train hard. Acclimate progressively. Hydrate appropriately. Don’t be an idiot.

results.transcript: Any runners struggling in the heat, this video is going to change your life. Heat training is one of the most important tools in a runner's toolbox. I'm going to talk about the benefits, but most importantly, my top five tips after racing ultras in Arizona where it's 99 degrees, Ironmans in Cozumel, and racing this weekend, my sixth ultra this year alone, where it's going to be 100 degrees. So let's talk about the benefits before I tell you the tips. And if I left anything out, please drop it in the comments. Let's help the community best as possible. The biggest thing with heat training, it's a performance enhancer. Increased blood plasma volume. It's basically an EPO. It lowers your heart rate at the same effort. You sweat earlier and more efficiently. You better regulate your core temperature and way more improved performance. If you do it right, and this is exactly how you do it. When it comes to heat training, the top five tips that I tell all my athletes, what I told myself going into 90, 100 degree weather, slow your pace. Forget your watch, run by effort, not pace. Because the heat makes the pace harder. Why? Your body is sending more blood to your skin to get rid of the heat, leaving less available blood for your muscles. So if your easy pace is at eight, kick it back to nine. That is okay. What matters is consistency. Second, you need to hydrate. Not just during your run, but outside of your run. I talk about this in every video. Why? Runners are always dehydrated. Find your sweat rate, find your sodium loss, and replenish it throughout the day, not just the run. Three, you need to be okay accepting a higher heart rate. Why? Your heart is working harder to cool you. A higher heart rate in the heat is normal. Don't just forget that your heart has to work harder to cool itself off. Thus, it's going to beat faster at an easier pace. Four, the biggest tip that I can say, cold water, ice bandanas, and make sure that you're wearing stuff that is very breathable. That is it. You don't want to trap the sweat. You don't want to trap the heat. But ice bandanas are going to save your life. Five, you need to start with 30 to 45 minutes at an easy pace. Do not just jump right into a double threshold. You could potentially get injured. And two, it's not going to end well. The goal here is to adapt to it. Most runners spend the summer hiding from the heat, but the best runners when it comes down to race day are the ones that train in the summer months, absorb all the training, better their performance because heat training after 7 to 14 days acts as a natural performance enhancer. This is a very big thing a lot of runners avoid, especially speed training because they can't hit their pace and sometimes their ego gets in the way. Understand that not hitting your pace during the heat is okay. What's not okay is training during it. These are my top five tips. I have so many others. So if people are curious, drop them in the comments. I'll do a lot of videos, but understand that heat training is normal. It is very, very efficient if you do it correctly and there's tips and tricks to actually enjoy it. So whatever I left out, please leave in the comments. Other than that, guys, be safe, hydrate, stay cool and happy running. I'm out of here.
